_meta.schema: DESIGN.md section 10.2-10.3. Every option writes into channels the engine already understands.
_meta.note: Costs are % of GDP per year unless stated. reformIndex is 0-100 and feeds the reform stock. Political fit is -1..+1 per party and drives the House vote (POLITICS.md).
_meta.sources: See RESEARCH note in POLICIES.md. Figures are from reporting current to August 2026 and should be re-checked before publication.
_meta.flags: Options may declare `requires` (flags that must be set for the card to appear), `sets` and `clears`. This is what makes cancellation prune a branch and open another - DESIGN.md section 10.3. Flags set at scenario start represent the February 2026 inheritance.
_meta.dependsOn: An option may declare dependsOn: {flag, withoutFactor, note}. If the flag is not set, the option's effects are scaled by withoutFactor. This is how one reform becomes the precondition for another actually working, rather than merely being described that way in the briefing.
_meta.requiresFlags: An option may declare requiresFlags: [...] — a HARD prerequisite. The option is shown locked until every flag is set. Distinct from dependsOn, which is a soft discount. Together these form the tech tree: Digital Government -> Civil Service Reform; Super Licence -> OECD accession; VAT Reform -> Negative Income Tax.

policies.name: Super Licence and Omnibus Law
policies.briefing: Replace sequential ministry-by-ministry approvals with a single unified licence, and consolidate up to 7,000 overlapping business rules. Target: super licence live within 180 days, full omnibus consolidation within a year. Almost no fiscal cost. It removes the slowest approving agency from the critical path, which is exactly why the slowest approving agencies resist it.

options.label: Full omnibus consolidation
options.flavour: The cheapest real reform available. Costs almost nothing and almost nobody in your coalition wants it.

dependsOn.note: A unified licence is meaningless if ministries cannot see each other's records. Without whole-of-government digital migration the omnibus delivers barely half its effect.

options.label: Super licence only, defer the omnibus
options.flavour: Half the reform, a third of the enemies.

options.label: Take no action
options.flavour: Seven thousand overlapping rules, left exactly where they are. The ministries that wrote them will be relieved.

policies.name: OECD Accession
policies.briefing: Thailand submitted its Initial Memorandum in December 2025 and is in technical review. Accession requires alignment across competition policy, state enterprise governance, anti-corruption, investment openness and corporate governance. It is the single most demanding reform programme available, it costs almost nothing fiscally, and none of it delivers inside one parliamentary term.

options.label: Accelerate the roadmap
options.flavour: Every chapter is a fight with a ministry that likes things as they are. The payoff arrives in the 2030s.
options.lockedNote: Requires the Super Licence. OECD investment-openness chapters cannot be answered while approvals still run ministry by ministry.

options.label: Proceed at technical pace
options.flavour: Progress reports, working groups, no confrontations.

options.label: Let it drift
options.flavour: The working groups continue. The chapters do not. Everyone understands what has happened without anyone saying it.

policies.name: Civil Service Reform
policies.briefing: 1.8 million core civil servants, 3.0 million including teachers, medical staff, police and military. Personnel and pensions consume roughly 1.4 trillion baht — close to a third of total budget expenditure, and the Parliamentary Budget Office wants it capped at 35% by 2032. The plan on the desk cuts the core workforce by about a third, to 1.35 million, through voluntary early retirement aimed at officials around 40 — some 414,000 people, 30% of the workforce, young enough to retrain. No compulsion, financial incentives plus reskilling, targeted for fiscal 2027. The severance is paid now; the savings arrive over a decade. The public wage bill is downward-rigid, and this is the only card that moves it.

options.label: Full early-retirement programme

lag.note: severance now, wage bill relief from 2029

options.flavour: You are asking the bureaucracy to vote for its own reduction. Every ministry will find a reason its own establishment is the exception, and Others — the institutional bloc — will not forgive it. They are also the people who implement everything else you pass.
options.lockedNote: Requires Digital Government. The state cannot shed a third of its staff until something automates what they did.

options.label: Freeze hiring, let attrition do it
options.flavour: Slower, cheaper, survivable. Roughly a decade to achieve what the full scheme does in four.

options.label: Leave the establishment alone
options.flavour: A third of the budget, untouched, growing.

policies.name: Ministry Restructure — Tourism, Culture and Sport
policies.briefing: The Office of the Public Sector Development Commission has a framework in front of cabinet: cleave sport out of the Ministry of Tourism and Sports into a ministry of its own, and merge what remains into a Ministry of Culture and Tourism. The argument is soft power — that Thailand sells culture and has been administering it in a department attached to football. The counter-argument is that machinery-of-government changes consume eighteen months of senior attention and deliver an org chart. Tourism was 2.7 trillion baht in 2025 across foreign and domestic, on arrivals that fell 7.2% while everyone waited for the Chinese market to come back.

options.label: Split sport out and merge tourism with culture
options.flavour: Two new permanent secretaries, one genuine strategic alignment, and a year and a half of everybody arguing about which department keeps which budget line. The soft-power case is real. So is the disruption.

options.label: Create the sports ministry, leave tourism where it is
options.flavour: The half of the reform with a constituency behind it. Sport gets its own budget; tourism keeps the letterhead it has always had.

options.label: Leave the machinery alone
options.flavour: There is a serious argument that reorganising ministries is what governments do when they cannot think of a policy.

policies.name: Party Finance and Organisation Act
policies.briefing: The networks are gone and the party still has to fight an election. The Political Party Development Fund shared 117 million baht across 77 parties in 2020 — thirteen to seventeen million each for the large ones, which pays for an office, not a campaign. The allocation formula has weighted votes at 40%, membership dues at 40% and branches at 20% since 2017, and it is gamed: branches that exist on paper until the audit, members enrolled without their knowledge, subsidies drawn against both. That formula is already the instrument. A big house delivers votes without members and without branches, so enforcing the weights it already has moves money from machines to organisations — and this is the one parliament in which the governing party has no machine left to protect.

options.label: Enforce the formula, audit the branches, fund against projects
options.flavour: Dues and branches decide the money, disbursement is against audited projects rather than a lump sum, and constituency spending is capped. None of it is new law so much as the existing law meant seriously. Parties that are organisations gain; parties that are a name attached to thirty families lose, and two of those are sitting in this parliament.

options.label: Enlarge the fund, leave the formula alone
options.flavour: More money through the same formula, which every party welcomes precisely because it changes nothing. The ghost branches draw a larger subsidy than they did last year.

options.label: Not this parliament
options.flavour: The party has renounced patronage finance and has not replaced it, which is a condition with a name and a short life expectancy.

policies.name: Negative Income Tax
policies.briefing: Replace the patchwork of subsidies with a single income-tested transfer, targeted for 2027. Threshold around 60,000 baht a year. Only 10 million of 67 million Thais currently file, so the scheme requires mass enrolment into the tax net — which is the point, and the problem. The Finance Ministry has paired it with a VAT rise above 7% to fund it.

options.label: Implement, funded from general revenue
options.flavour: Broadens the tax base by making 20 million people file for the first time. They will notice. Funding it properly means the VAT card.
options.lockedNote: Requires a revenue measure — VAT Reform or the Revenue Mobilisation Package. A transfer to twenty million new filers cannot be funded from a base flat at 21% of GDP.

options.label: Transfers without the VAT rise
options.flavour: All of the cost, none of the funding. Popular, and the debt ceiling is already at 70%.

dependsOn.note: Unfunded by design — the debt does the funding.

options.label: Defer to the next government
options.flavour: Everyone agrees it should happen. Nobody agrees it should happen now.

policies.name: Thai Chuay Thai Plus
policies.briefing: Co-payment stimulus: 1,000 baht a month for four months to roughly 30 million Thais aged 18 and over, spendable only within the month. Around 120 billion baht, 0.63% of GDP. The multiplier on direct transfers is 0.30 — the weakest instrument in the fiscal toolkit — and at 87.5% household debt a meaningful share goes to repayment rather than spending.

options.label: Run the full scheme
options.flavour: Everyone gets a thousand baht and remembers who gave it to them. It buys four months of goodwill and nothing else.

options.label: Means-test to the bottom 40%
options.flavour: Twice the multiplier per baht, a fraction of the gratitude.

options.label: Redirect the funds to public investment
options.flavour: The government did this once before, moving 157 billion baht out of the Digital Wallet. Multiplier 0.30 becomes 0.675. Nobody thanks you.

policies.name: Thailand Individual Savings Account (TISA)
policies.briefing: Tax-advantaged savings accounts for Thai equities, approved December 2025. Deduction up to 800,000 baht; those earning under 1.5 million baht may deduct up to 1.3 times their contribution. Targets roughly 11.4 million income earners. Deepens the domestic capital market and supports the SET — but the deduction is regressive, since only the 10 million who file benefit at all.

options.label: Launch as approved
options.flavour: Deepens the capital market. The benefit lands almost entirely on people who already file taxes.

options.label: Equalise deduction rights across income bands
options.flavour: Fairer, more expensive, and the brokerages stop returning your calls.

options.label: Shelve it
options.flavour: The capital market stays shallow and the 11.4 million people who file keep their money in deposits.

policies.name: VAT Reform
policies.briefing: VAT has sat at 7% for over three decades, renewed by royal decree year after year, against a statutory 10%. The Finance Ministry's published path is 8.5% in 2028 and 10% in 2030, alongside a 1 baht per litre fuel excise rise from 2027, targeting revenue of 15.1% of GDP and a deficit under 3% by FY2029. Each percentage point is worth roughly 0.55% of GDP. The tax multiplier is -1.125 - the largest in the toolkit - so every baht raised costs more output than a baht of spending gains, and it lands immediately while the spending it funds does not. If the House will not wear it, the Revenue Mobilisation Package raises about two-thirds as much without putting anyone on the street.

options.label: Keep VAT at 7%
options.flavour: The thirty-fourth consecutive year of the temporary reduction.

options.label: Phased: 8.5% in 2028, 10% in 2030
options.flavour: The published plan. Half the revenue arrives after the next election, which is rather the point.

options.label: Go straight to 10%
options.flavour: Closes the fiscal gap in one move, funds everything else on this desk, and hands the opposition a slogan that writes itself. -1.65pp of output on impact.

policies.name: Revenue Mobilisation Package
policies.briefing: The unglamorous half of the Finance Ministry's plan, and the half nobody campaigns against: a 1 baht per litre fuel excise from 2027, tighter excise on alcohol, tobacco and vehicles, a cap on personal income tax deductions, and — the largest single item — closing the gap between tax assessed and tax collected. Only 10 million of 67 million Thais file at all. None of it raises as much as three points on VAT, and none of it puts anyone on the street. It is what a government does when it cannot get VAT through the House, which is most governments, most of the time.

options.label: Full package — excise, deduction caps, collection

dependsOn.note: Most of the yield is better collection, not higher rates — and the Revenue Department cannot collect what it cannot see. Without whole-of-government digital migration this delivers well under two-thirds.

options.flavour: Two-thirds of the revenue of a phased VAT rise, a fraction of the fight. The people who notice are the ones who were not paying.

options.label: Fuel and sin excise only
options.flavour: The path of least resistance. Enough to unlock the transfer programme, not enough to fund it comfortably.

options.label: No revenue measure
options.flavour: Revenue stays at 21% of GDP, where it has been for a decade.

policies.name: Central Cooperative Debt Consolidation

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Kla Tham's price for its fifty-eight seats is the rural credit agenda it was built on.

policies.briefing: 6,092 cooperatives, 11 million members, and savings cooperatives alone holding between 2.27 and 2.7 trillion baht of loans — roughly 15% of all Thai household debt. Six of 1,369 savings cooperatives report to the credit bureau, so nobody can see a member's total obligations. Salary deduction at source means the cooperative is paid before the member eats, which removes any incentive to restructure. The proposal is a single central body to absorb and restructure farmer and teacher cooperative debt, with credit bureau reporting made mandatory as the price of entry.

options.label: Create the central body, with mandatory credit-bureau reporting
options.flavour: The reporting requirement is worth more than the restructuring: you cannot fix a debt problem you cannot measure, and 1,363 of these institutions currently lend blind. The cooperative boards will fight it, because dividends are paid out of exactly the interest rates this exposes.

options.label: Leave the cooperatives to the registrar
options.flavour: The Cooperative Promotion Department has supervised this sector into 15% of national household debt. It will continue to.

policies.name: The People's Bank

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Kla Tham's price for its fifty-eight seats is the rural credit agenda it was built on.

policies.briefing: A state bank for micro-loans at capped, below-market rates. The case for it is that household debt has passed 86% of GDP and the informal lenders charging the bottom decile are the reason a large part of it never amortises. The case against is every state credit institution Thailand has built: they lend to the politically legible rather than the creditworthy, capped rates ration by queue rather than price, and the losses arrive on the sovereign balance sheet several years after the government that created them has gone.

options.label: Charter the bank with capped rates
options.flavour: Ten points of approval and a contingent liability nobody will price until it defaults. If it displaces the informal lenders it is the best thing in this section; if it becomes a channel for directed credit it is the Krung Thai story again, and the second is what usually happens.

options.label: Expand the existing state banks' mandate instead
options.flavour: GSB and BAAC already do this, badly, and at least their losses are already on the books.

policies.name: Senior Plus 1 — Employment Incentive
policies.briefing: Thailand became an aged society in 2024 and will be super-aged by 2033, when 18.4 million people are over 60 and the elderly outnumber children. The country grew grey before it grew rich, which is the whole problem: the labour force is shrinking under an economy that never reached high income. A corporate deduction already exists — 200% of wages paid to Thai employees over 60 — but it is capped at salaries of 15,000 baht a month and at 10% of a firm's headcount, which confines it to the lowest-paid work an older worker can do. Senior Plus 1 doubles the salary ceiling to 30,000 and asks whether the headcount cap should survive.

options.label: Double the ceiling to 30,000 baht and lift the headcount cap
options.flavour: Revenue forgone now against a participation rate that compounds for a decade. The headcount cap is the binding constraint, not the salary ceiling — a firm that wants to staff a shift with people over 60 currently cannot.

options.label: Raise the ceiling only, keep the 10% headcount cap
options.flavour: Better-paid work for the older workers firms already employ, and no more of them.

policies.name: Senior Plus 2 — Income Tax Relief
policies.briefing: The employer side is done; the worker side is untouched. A Thai over 60 who keeps working pays income tax at the same schedule as everyone else, on top of losing means-tested support, so the effective marginal rate on staying in work is punitive at exactly the income where the decision is finely balanced. Senior Plus 2 grants a deduction of up to 50% for earners over 60 with assessable income under 1.5 million baht a year — which is to say, for almost all of them.

options.label: Grant the full 50% deduction under 1.5 million baht
options.flavour: The most expensive of the three and the one that actually changes a household's arithmetic. Note the second effect: income that was never declared because declaring it cost more than hiding it starts appearing on returns.

options.label: A limited 25% deduction, reviewed after two years
options.flavour: Half the cost and rather less than half the behavioural response — the review date is itself a reason not to reorganise your working life around it.

policies.name: Land Bridge (Chumphon–Ranong)
policies.briefing: The Southern Economic Corridor land bridge. Over one trillion baht, Phase 1 targeted to open 2030 with full completion around 2035. Proponents project a transformational logistics shortcut past the Malacca Strait. Critics note the transfer would take roughly 54 hours against 48 through Malacca, cost around US$252 more per container, and that 73.9% of Thai trade already uses regional routes with little incentive to switch.

options.label: Push ahead with Phase 1

lag.note: Nothing lands before 2031. Outside the window.

options.flavour: The southern provinces get a decade of construction. You get the bill and none of the ribbon.

dependsOn.note: Without a revenue measure this is pure borrowing against a ceiling already within five points.

options.label: Delay pending review
options.flavour: Preserves the option and the money, and reads as prudence rather than retreat. The file comes back in two quarters and you will have to answer then.

options.label: Cancel outright
options.flavour: Honest arithmetic, expensive politics. The southern corridor does not disappear - a rail-only link becomes the obvious consolation prize.

policies.name: Chumphon–Ranong Rail Link
policies.briefing: With the Land Bridge cancelled, the southern corridor reverts to what the corridor was always going to justify on its own: a conventional rail link between the Gulf and the Andaman coasts. A fraction of the cost, a fraction of the ambition, and unlike the deep-sea ports it does not depend on persuading global shippers to abandon Malacca. It also gives the southern provinces something to point at after you took away the trillion-baht project.

options.label: Build the rail link
options.flavour: Roughly a third of Land Bridge Phase 1, and it might actually carry something.

options.label: Commission a feasibility study
options.flavour: The traditional Thai response to a corridor that will not pencil out.

options.label: Leave the corridor alone
options.flavour: Two cancellations in the same region. The South will remember.

policies.name: Northeast HSR — Bangkok–Nong Khai (Phase 2)
policies.briefing: Phase 2 of the Thai–Chinese high-speed railway: Nakhon Ratchasima to Nong Khai, 357 km, around US$10.1 billion, targeted operational 2030 and connecting into the China–Laos line. Phase 1 has already slipped a year. It is the largest single capital commitment available, it is geopolitically loaded, and the completion date sits precisely at the end of your term - which means the ribbon, if there is one, belongs to whoever wins in 2030.

options.label: Fund Phase 2 and accelerate
options.flavour: Isan gets a railway to China. The budget gets a hole until 2033.

dependsOn.note: Without a revenue measure this is pure borrowing against a ceiling already within five points.

options.label: Finish Phase 1, defer Phase 2
options.flavour: Deliver something before promising more. Unfashionable.

options.label: Renegotiate financing terms with Beijing
options.flavour: Better terms, slower delivery, and a conversation nobody in the ministry wants to have.

policies.name: Eastern HSR — Three-Airport Link
policies.briefing: Don Mueang–Suvarnabhumi–U-Tapao, the spine of the Eastern Economic Corridor. Eight years late, over 21.8 billion baht already sunk - 9.8bn of it public, on land expropriation and utility relocation - and the concession faces a review that can end it outright. Sites were never handed over cleanly, a drainage channel at Makkasan is still unresolved, U-Tapao passenger forecasts have been cut, and the concessionaire cannot close financing against that uncertainty. Termination means negotiating compensation for money already spent on both sides.

options.label: Amend the concession and proceed
options.flavour: Eight years of delay rewarded with better terms. The Democrats will read the file aloud.

options.label: Terminate the concession
options.flavour: Compensation talks, a decade of nothing to show for 21.8 billion baht, and every foreign concessionaire in Thailand rereading their termination clauses.

options.label: Defer the review again
options.flavour: The ninth year.

policies.name: EEC Conventional Rail (post-termination)
policies.briefing: With the high-speed concession dead, the corridor still needs a spine. Conventional double-track electrified rail to U-Tapao delivers most of the freight and commuter case at a fraction of the cost, on a timetable that fits inside a parliamentary term. It is the sensible answer, and it is an admission that eight years and 21.8 billion baht bought a lesson.

options.label: Build conventional double-track to U-Tapao
options.flavour: Lands inside your term. Nobody makes a documentary about double-track.

options.label: Re-tender the high-speed line
options.flavour: Same project, new consortium, same drainage channel at Makkasan.

options.label: No replacement
options.flavour: Twenty-one billion baht, eight years, and an empty corridor. The EEC keeps the name.

policies.name: Electric Bus Network
policies.briefing: The BMTA carries 150 billion baht of accumulated debt and loses 8 billion a year. It also runs a fleet old enough that replacing it is not optional. 1,520 electric buses are due by March 2027, with Cabinet approving a further 800 on lease for 8.14 billion baht and 700 more replacing NGV stock at 7.1 billion. Leasing rather than buying keeps it off the capital budget; electric running costs are where the loss actually narrows. Fares are held so commuting stays under a fifth of the minimum wage, which is the entire political point and the entire fiscal problem.

options.label: Full fleet electrification and route overhaul

dependsOn.note: Route rationalisation and integrated ticketing need the data the BMTA does not currently hold.

options.flavour: Visible within two years, which almost nothing else here is. Bangkok notices buses in a way it does not notice the Super Licence.

options.label: Lease the buses, leave the routes alone
options.flavour: New buses on the same bad routes. The photographs are identical and the losses continue.

options.label: Electrify and make it fare-free
options.flavour: The most approval per baht on this desk. It also permanently converts an 8 billion baht annual loss into a line item nobody can ever remove.

policies.name: Small Modular Reactors
policies.briefing: The Power Development Plan carries 600 MWe of small modular reactor capacity — two 300 MWe units, one in the Northeast and one in the South, commercial operation 2037. The Office of Atoms for Peace has existed since 1961 and has never licensed a power reactor; the legal framework for one is a chapter heading, not a code. Capital cost runs USD 5,000–10,000 per kW against an LCOE of USD 90–160/MWh, versus USD 79–86 for the gas you would otherwise burn. It is not cheap power. It is firm, low-carbon power on a grid that is 60% gas and importing most of it, and the cost curve only bends if somebody orders early. Every unit reaches first power well after you leave office.

options.label: Order both units and build the regulator

dependsOn.note: Vendor selection, fuel supply and the safeguards agreement all run through partners you have not aligned with.

options.flavour: You are paying a premium over gas for firm power that arrives in 2037, and standing up a nuclear regulator from a standing start. Both are correct. Neither is on a ballot paper you will ever contest.

options.label: Order one unit, site it in the Northeast
options.flavour: One unit is a demonstration, not a programme — it buys the regulator, the fuel agreement and the trained inspectors without betting the grid on a technology nobody has yet built at scale.

options.label: Fund the feasibility and siting study only
options.flavour: Three years of consultants and a public hearing in every candidate province. Defensible, cheap, and it hands the decision to the next government exactly as your predecessors handed it to you.

options.label: Strike the reactors from the plan
options.flavour: Uranium fever has done and got me down / Uranium fever it's spreadin' all around

policies.name: Semiconductor and Advanced Electronics
policies.briefing: Three years of roadmap have produced the one honest finding: Thailand cannot buy its way into wafer fabrication, and should stop pretending the question is money. What is reachable is the layer directly above where it sits now — advanced packaging, test, power and analogue devices, compliance-grade design services — and the engineering workforce to staff it. BOI's draft roadmap talks about 2.5 trillion baht of investment across the decade. None of that lands inside your term. What lands inside your term is whether the training pipeline, the design centres and the utility guarantees exist for somebody else to build on.

options.label: Fund the full package — packaging, design centres, 86,000 engineers

dependsOn.note: Without three years of a funded board there is no secretariat, no curriculum and no pipeline to accelerate — the programme starts from a standing start.

options.flavour: The most defensible use of public money on this desk and the one with the least to show for it by December 2030. Almost every number it moves is a number your successor gets to report.

options.label: Build a national champion around the sovereign programme
options.lockedNote: Requires a sovereign AI course — there is no national champion to build around without one.
options.flavour: State-directed, domestically owned, and answerable to you. It is also Alphatec's business plan with a larger budget, and everyone in the room is old enough to remember how that ended.

dependsOn.note: A champion with no domestic AI capacity to serve is a fabrication subsidy looking for a customer — the TH-AI redirect is what gives it demand.

options.label: Leave the sector to the BOI incentives already in place
options.flavour: More of the same. Assembly and test, priced against Vietnam, for as long as the wage gap holds.

policies.name: TH-AI Passport
policies.briefing: 1.6 billion baht from the Digital Economy fund giving five million Thais aged 15+ a year of access to twelve premium AI models, with mandatory upskilling. Fiscally trivial at 0.008% of GDP. Critics argue it subsidises foreign platforms, encourages passive consumption over critical skill, and deepens dependence on international providers, with questions raised over contractor selection.

options.label: Run the programme as designed
options.flavour: Costs almost nothing, polls well, and the productivity effect arrives after everyone in this room has retired.

options.label: Redirect toward domestic AI capacity
options.flavour: Builds something Thai instead of renting something American. Slower, and the procurement questions do not go away.

options.label: Cancel over procurement concerns
options.flavour: The procurement questions were fair. The five million people who were promised the tools will not read the audit.

policies.name: Digital Government
policies.briefing: The Digital Government Development Agency is consolidating ministries onto shared cloud infrastructure — e-Sarabun document handling with digital signatures and ThaiID authentication, e-Meeting, centralised data through the Government Data Cloud. Agencies are being onboarded one at a time and digital readiness varies enormously across the state. It is unglamorous, it is cheap, and it is the precondition for both civil service reduction and the Super Licence actually working: a unified permit is meaningless if the ministries cannot see each other's records.

options.label: Mandate whole-of-government migration
options.flavour: Raises budget execution more than any other card — the money you already allocate starts actually arriving. Every ministry will explain why it is a special case.

options.label: Continue voluntary agency onboarding
options.flavour: The agencies that were going to modernise anyway will modernise. The rest will not.

options.label: No additional push
options.flavour: Every ministry keeps its own database, its own signature, and its own reason why sharing is impossible.

policies.name: The 100-Baht Internet Package

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. The Democrats are the smallest party at the table and the only one with an institutional memory of governing.

policies.briefing: Thailand's mobile market consolidated to two operators of consequence, and prices have behaved exactly as an economist would predict. The Democrat proposal is a mandated 100-baht broadband package for low-income households, delivered through the universal service obligation rather than a subsidy cheque. It is a price control by another name, and the sector will say so loudly. It also puts a connection in the households that every digital government service you have built assumes already has one.

options.label: Mandate the package through the universal service obligation

dependsOn.note: Connectivity is only worth what there is to connect to — without the service migration this is a cheaper bill, not a capability.

options.flavour: Popular, cheap, and a genuine complement to everything you digitised. It is also the state setting a retail price in a licensed market, which the operators will litigate and the next investment round will remember.

options.label: Leave it to the regulator
options.flavour: The NBTC has been leaving it to the market since the merger. The market has noticed.

policies.name: Zero Corruption Act

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. The Economic Party holds three seats inside Others and one item of leverage: the FINAL EXIT programme it ran on.

policies.briefing: The Economic Party's ZERO CORRUPTION plank, and it is not a metaphor: capital punishment for public corruption, with execution mandated within one year of a Supreme Court verdict. Thai law already permits the death penalty for serious graft — the 2018 organic act extended it to foreign officials — and it has never once been carried out for it. What is new here is the mandate, which removes the discretion that has always been the point. Three seats of a right-libertarian party inside your coalition are asking, and they ran on this.

options.label: Pass the Act as drafted, mandatory execution and all
options.flavour: Do you dare have the gall to do this?

options.label: Take the enforcement, drop the death penalty
options.flavour: The most popular thing on this desk and the most dangerous. Enforcement with teeth does not primarily inconvenience the opposition — it reaches your own donors, your own provincial members and the people who deliver your seats. Institutional support does not fall because the establishment disapproves. It falls because you have begun prosecuting it.
options.lockedNote: Locked. Enforcement needs somewhere to land: an accelerated OECD accession that binds you to an external standard, and a civil service that has already been cut. Without both, an anti-corruption body is a new office in the same building, staffed by the same people.

options.label: Thank them and shelve it
options.flavour: The safe answer, and they will remember it at every subsequent division. Three seats is not many until the margin is three.

policies.name: Justice System Reform

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. The Economic Party holds three seats inside Others and one item of leverage: the FINAL EXIT programme it ran on.

policies.briefing: The second half of FINAL EXIT: uncouple arrest from investigation. Under the present arrangement the same police organisation that investigates a case also decides who is detained, which is the structural feature that lets protection networks convert enforcement into revenue. Separating the two — investigators who cannot arrest, prosecutors who direct the file — is the single most-recommended reform in every Thai policing review since 2007, and the single most consistently blocked.

options.label: Separate investigation from arrest, prosecutors direct the file
options.flavour: This is the reform that dissolves grey capital, and it is the reform the police have defeated for twenty years. Passing it costs you the one institution every Thai government needs quiet cooperation from, and buys an economy where the informal sector has a reason to formalise.
options.lockedNote: Locked until the Zero Corruption Act passes with real enforcement. Separating investigation from arrest without a body able to prosecute what it finds simply moves the bottleneck.

options.label: Pilot it in three provinces and review
options.flavour: A pilot is how this reform has been killed three times: it runs, it works, the review is scheduled after the next election, and nobody hears of it again.

options.label: Not this parliament
options.flavour: The Royal Thai Police are content, and so is everyone who has ever paid them.

policies.name: Migrant Labour Regularisation
policies.briefing: 3.65 million migrant workers are registered in Thailand, mostly from Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, and only about 1.4 million of them are inside the social security system. The government-to-government MOU channel has barely moved in a year — 635,000 to 655,000 — while the e-WorkPermit rollout of October 2025 failed badly enough to put over a million Myanmar workers at risk of falling out of legal status. The brokers price the gap: an agency renewal runs to tens of thousands of baht against under 4,000 done directly. When 300,000 Cambodians left over the border closures, the longan harvest alone lost an estimated 2.6 billion baht. This is the labour force the ageing projections quietly assume will keep showing up.

options.label: One-stop regularisation, brokers cut out, social security enrolment mandatory
options.flavour: The largest single move available on the formalisation channel and the most expensive thing on this desk politically. Building the one-stop system costs real money before a single contribution arrives, the enrolment revenue takes years to catch up with it, and the constituency you are taking the margin from is not a cartel of strangers — it is embedded in the ministries that would have to administer the replacement. Expect the whip count to be ugly and expect to lose approval you cannot buy back.

options.label: Widen the MOU channel and leave the rest alone
options.flavour: Doubles a channel that carries a fifth of the workforce. The brokers keep the other four fifths, which is where their margin was always coming from.

options.label: Enforcement first — raids, fines, deportations
options.flavour: Popular, straightforward, and it drives the workforce further underground rather than out of the country — the farms and the building sites still need them next season. Ask the longan growers what a labour shortage costs.

policies.name: Tourism Workforce Reskilling
policies.briefing: The stated ambition is up to 10 million tourism-related jobs, supported by free state-backed upskilling in digital tourism, hospitality standards and AI. It sits inside the five-ministry human-capital strategy the government has already announced, which is coordinated across Labour, Education, Higher Education, Social Development and Agriculture and which conspicuously has not been costed. Tourism is the country's largest employer of people without a degree, its productivity per worker is among the lowest in the economy, and the sector is about to be reorganised by exactly the technologies the curriculum is meant to teach.

options.label: Fund the full programme with a credit-bank qualification behind it

dependsOn.note: delivered through five ministries that cannot see each other's records

options.flavour: Ten million jobs is a number from a press release; the programme underneath it is five ministries, an uncosted strategy and a credit bank that does not exist yet. Human capital is the slowest channel in the model and this is the last quarter it can be started in, so essentially none of the return lands before the election — you are spending real money in your final year on an outcome your successor collects. Without digital government underneath it, most of it dissipates between the five ministries running it.

options.label: Hospitality standards only, no digital component
options.flavour: The training the industry asks for, which is the training it has always asked for, and which leaves the workforce exactly as exposed to automation as it was.

options.label: The sector trains its own
options.flavour: It does, informally, on the job, to no standard anybody can put on a CV.

policies.name: High-Value Agriculture

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Pheu Thai's constituency is agricultural, and it has not had a farm policy of its own since rice pledging.

policies.briefing: Roughly a third of Thai employment is still agricultural and it produces under a tenth of output, which is the arithmetic behind every income statistic in the country. The proposal is to move the sector up the value chain rather than subsidise it down: precision farming, synthetic biology and biorefining under the BCG framework already declared a national agenda, contract standards that let smallholders access it, and net-zero targets to open the European market. It is the anti-rice-pledging — the same constituency, the opposite instrument.

options.label: Fund the full transition — precision farming, biorefining, standards

dependsOn.note: Traceability and contract standards run on registries the ministry does not currently hold.

options.flavour: The most defensible thing any Thai government has proposed for agriculture in twenty years, and the slowest: a smallholder converting to high-value production needs three seasons and credit, and you are offering one of the two.

options.label: Input subsidies and a price floor instead
options.flavour: Twelve points of approval and the entire lesson of 2011 to 2014 discarded to get them. The farm vote is real and this is what it costs to buy rather than earn.

options.label: Leave the sector to the existing schemes
options.flavour: Thirty per cent of the workforce, eight per cent of output, and no plan. It has been the position of every government since 2014.

policies.name: Converting Sor Por Kor Land Deeds

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Kla Tham's price for its fifty-eight seats is the rural credit agenda it was built on.

policies.briefing: 1.62 million farmers hold 22.07 million rai on Sor Por Kor 4-01 documents — land they may farm and may not borrow against. The legislation to convert those documents into title has been drafted since Thamanat drove it from the agriculture ministry: five years' cultivation required, transfers restricted to other eligible farmers, and the resulting deed usable as bank collateral. That last clause is the entire policy. It is also the entire risk: Thailand has run land reform programmes before, and the land has a way of ending up with people who were never eligible for it.

options.label: Convert the documents to full title deeds
options.flavour: Twenty-two million rai of dead capital converted into collateral, which is the single largest formalisation available to any Thai government. The transfer restrictions are the only thing standing between that and a land grab, and transfer restrictions have historically lasted about as long as the government that wrote them.

options.label: Leave the documents as they are
options.flavour: The safest answer, and it leaves 1.62 million households farming land they cannot borrow against in a country where credit is the binding constraint on every farm upgrade.

policies.name: Mental Health in the Universal Scheme

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Universal coverage is Pheu Thai's founding achievement and it would like a second chapter.

policies.briefing: Thailand has 1.3 psychiatrists per 100,000 people against a global average of 13. Roughly 13.4 million Thais report a mental health condition; 89% received no care in the past year and 8.2% got formal treatment. The Department of Mental Health runs on 1.8% of the public health budget. The universal coverage scheme is the delivery mechanism Thailand already has and the only one that reaches the provinces — the proposal is to write mental health into it properly, with a training pipeline attached, because the workforce is the binding constraint and it takes six years to build.

options.label: Write it into the scheme and fund the training pipeline
options.flavour: Cheap by the standards of this desk and slow by the standards of any electorate — the psychiatrists you fund today qualify after you have left office. The lost output from untreated illness in the working-age population is larger than the programme, which is the argument nobody makes because it sounds callous.

options.label: Not in this budget
options.flavour: The Department of Mental Health keeps its 1.8%. Nobody protests, because the constituency for this is by definition not organised.

policies.name: Senior Plus 3 — One Village, One Volunteer Nurse
policies.briefing: Tax relief does nothing for the third of the elderly population who cannot work. Thailand's answer to rural health has always been the village health volunteer — roughly a million of them, the network that carried the country through COVID — but they are volunteers with a stipend and a fortnight of training, and ageing-in-place needs a clinician. One Village, One Volunteer Nurse puts a qualified nurse behind the volunteer network in each of some 75,000 villages, working proactively rather than waiting at a district hospital for an emergency that a home visit would have prevented.

options.label: Fund the nationwide programme and the training pipeline
options.flavour: The binding constraint is nurses, not money, and nurses take four years — most of this programme is delivered by the government after yours. Proactive community care is the single cheapest thing a super-aged country can do, and the saving lands as an avoided hospital admission nobody will ever attribute to you.

options.label: Limit it to the twenty oldest provinces
options.flavour: Targets the need accurately and guarantees that the other fifty-seven provinces read about it in the newspaper.

policies.name: Fully Funded 15-Year Education

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. The Democrats are the smallest party at the table and the only one with an institutional memory of governing.

policies.briefing: Fifteen years of free schooling has been policy since 2009 and it is the Democrats' own — the party wrote it in government and would now like it to be true. The state pays a per-head subsidy and families pay for transport, materials, registration and credential fees, which is why households under 2,802 baht a month still drop children out at the grade 6-7 and 9-10 transitions. The per-head formula also quietly punishes small rural schools, which receive less precisely because they are small. The proposal is to fund the whole cost to the household and reweight the subsidy toward remote schools.

options.label: Fund it properly — materials, transport, fees, and a remote-school weighting
options.flavour: The highest human-capital return on this desk and the slowest: a child kept in school through the grade 9 transition this year enters the labour force in 2038. Every finance minister since 2009 has agreed with the policy and funded the subsidy rather than the cost.

options.label: Keep the existing per-head subsidy
options.flavour: It has been called free for seventeen years. One more will not be noticed by anyone who is not paying for it.

policies.name: Vulnerable Demographic Allowances

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Palang Pracharath sits inside Others, is short of a cause, and has always been strongest with the elderly vote.

policies.briefing: The old-age allowance is still tiered by age — 600 baht a month at 60, rising to 1,000 only at 90 — and the child support grant reaches a fraction of those eligible. Thailand passed 'aged society' status years ago and will be 'super-aged' inside a decade, which makes this the one spending line that grows whether or not anyone legislates. The proposal is a flat 1,000 baht for everyone over 60 and a widened maternal grant. It is popular, it is defensible, and it is permanent.

options.label: Flat 1,000 baht at 60, and widen the maternal grant
options.flavour: The most reliable eleven points of approval available anywhere on this desk. It is also a permanent claim on the budget in a country whose dependency ratio is deteriorating faster than almost any middle-income peer — you are not buying four years of goodwill, you are buying it for your successors as well.

options.label: Keep the existing tiers
options.flavour: Fiscally correct and politically friendless. The 600-baht rate has not moved in real terms in over a decade, and every year it does not move is a transfer from the old to the bond market.

policies.name: Provincial Tourism Allocations
policies.briefing: The Tourism Promotion Fund holds 10 billion baht. The proposal is to hand 100 million of it to each of the 77 provinces — 7.7 billion in total — earmarked for local festivals, cultural events and regional activity, on the reasoning that foreign arrivals concentrate in five provinces while the fund is national. Domestic tourism was 1.16 trillion baht last year and grew while the foreign side fell 4.7%, so the demand is genuinely there. Whether an equal split finds it is a different question: Mae Hong Son and Chon Buri receive the same envelope.

options.label: One hundred million to every province, no conditions
options.flavour: Seventy-seven governors with a budget line and a ribbon. Politically this is close to free money and economically it is close to a transfer — the provinces that can absorb it productively are not the ones the formula was designed to help.

options.label: Allocate against submitted proposals, audited afterwards
options.flavour: Better spending and considerably worse politics. Every province that loses a round will explain that the criteria were written in Bangkok, and they will not be entirely wrong.

options.label: Keep the fund centralised
options.flavour: The fund continues to be spent on campaigns in the five provinces that were always going to be full.
